title: Model finite Elmer's glue joint strength
description: The current truss treats every glued node as ideal/infinite strength, so only wooden members fail. Add a finite glue-to-wood joint failure model using a documented, defensible Elmer's glue strength relative to the modeled toothpick wood strength. Joint failures must be visible in the load test and trigger deterministic load redistribution/cascading failure.
design: Research the specific Elmer's product/strength data before choosing the default ratio; distinguish published values from an illustrative calibration because adhesive strength depends on species, overlap area, surface prep, cure, and load direction. Make the assumed bond geometry and strength ratio explicit/configurable. Keep this educational, not an engineering prediction. Sequence after evolving geometry so joint capacity uses its actual member geometry.
acceptance_criteria: A documented Elmer's glue preset has finite strength relative to the modeled toothpick wood; the UI lets users inspect/change the glue-vs-wood setting and identifies whether wood or glue caused each failure. Joint capacity is evaluated at member endpoints using explicit geometry/load assumptions, and failed bonds remove the connected member end and re-solve the truss deterministically. Tests cover wood-governed failure, glue-governed failure, mixed/cascading failures, determinism, and any geometry-dependent capacity. README and UI clearly qualify data and assumptions.
notes:
Source check: Pi Symphony's white-glue test (http://www.pisymphony.com/toothpick/GLUETEST/gluetest.html) tested 50 simple 0.4-inch-overlap joints using five wood-glue products, including two Elmer's and three Titebond variants. It reports only the overall specimen range (12–39 lbf), not per-product results; it is not a product-specific Elmer's School Glue specification. Therefore Gemini's attribution of that range to an Elmer's toothpick joint and its use of generic 3,600–4,000 psi wood-glue claims are not verified. Treat 53–173 N as a broad, illustrative empirical range only; require a clearly labeled/configurable calibration and avoid claiming an authoritative Elmer's ratio unless better data is found.
Implementation calibration: the control defaults to 0.44× the modeled 120 N wood tensile capacity (~53 N), the low end of the mixed-product 12–39 lbf range; it is user-adjustable through 1.44× (~173 N). The UI calls this an Elmer's-style white/PVA illustration and explicitly says the source is not product-specific. Each member end assumes a fixed 0.4-inch lap, with axial tensile member force as bond demand; compression is handled by the wood/buckling model. Failed bond records its endpoint and removes the attached member before re-solving.
Verification complete: 27 automated tests pass. Chromium desktop/mobile QA confirmed 24 visibly distinct geometries, fixed toothpick counts, glue-strength interaction and save/restore, glue-failure endpoint/status rendering, no console exceptions, and no horizontal overflow at 375 px. Product-specific glue strength remains unknown; UI/README describe this as an illustrative low-end calibration rather than a measured Elmer's strength.
close_reason: Implemented an adjustable finite glue-end model (0.44–1.44× wood tension), documented the mixed-product evidence limitations, persisted the setting, and exposed wood/glue failure causes in playback/UI. Added deterministic wood, glue, mixed-population, worker, persistence, and cascade tests; full suite passes and Chromium QA is clean.

title: Evolve bridge geometry and triangle proportions
description: Extend the bridge genome beyond choosing reinforcement members on a fixed triangular lattice. Evolve node positions and triangle sizes/angles while preserving the fixed support span and deterministic static truss simulation. Enforce a strict member-length maximum below one toothpick and a hard total budget of 40 members/toothpicks per bridge; every shorter segment still consumes one budget unit.
design: Treat member lengths as geometric segment lengths strictly less than one toothpick (with a numerical safety margin); count each segment as one whole toothpick regardless of unused length, so the 40-stick limit is conservative. Keep supports and center load anchored at the same fixed span. Genome operators must preserve or repair valid connected, triangulated bridges and remain deterministic. Strength/buckling continues to use actual member length.
acceptance_criteria: Seeded runs reproducibly evolve visibly different triangle dimensions and shapes, not just reinforcement toggles. Every generated bridge preserves the support span, uses at most 40 member segments, and every segment/triangle side is strictly shorter than one toothpick. Candidates remain connected and structurally testable; mutation/crossover do not cause invalid coordinates or non-finite solver inputs. Unit and property tests cover bounds, deterministic evolution, geometry changes, solver behavior for unequal member lengths, and budget compliance; UI and README explain the variable-size/toothpick-count model.
close_reason: Implemented deterministic variable-geometry genome, 39-member connected triangulated bridge, strict sub-toothpick length and 40-stick budget validation, geometry-aware solver/rendering/worker/persistence, documentation, and regression coverage (24 tests pass).

title: Render load ramp, member stress, breakage, and replay
description: Render the selected candidate bridge on Canvas 2D as its hanging weight increases. Communicate load, member stress, each break/cascade, and final collapse; allow a completed candidate or champion to be replayed.
design: Use Canvas 2D with device-pixel-ratio-aware sizing. Keep simulation evaluation separate from animation: the solver supplies a break-event timeline and the renderer interpolates the weight between events. Support a reduced-motion mode that still exposes the same numeric state.
acceptance_criteria: The load visibly rises through solver break events; members are visually differentiated by tension/compression/stress state; failed members visibly separate or disappear; the final stable load and failure state are shown; replay uses recorded deterministic failure events and does not mutate the candidate.
close_reason: Added Canvas truss rendering, stress/buckling color cues, broken-member gaps, load interpolation from immutable failure events, replay, and reduced-motion pacing.

title: Add structural solver and failure regression tests
description: Add automated tests for equilibrium, supports, force signs, capacity limits, cascades, instability, and deterministic results so the simulation can evolve without silently changing its meaning.
design: Keep the mechanics tests independent of browser rendering. Prefer the platform test runner or a small dependency-free harness that fits the chosen static-module setup.
acceptance_criteria: Tests cover at least a simply supported test truss with a known reaction, a tension failure, a compression/buckling failure, a post-break redistribution/cascade, an unstable bridge, and repeatable seeded evaluation; tests run from a documented command.
close_reason: The dependency-free Node tests cover support reactions, member signs, tension/buckling, instability, redistribution after failure, and deterministic evaluations; npm test passes.

title: Implement the seeded genetic algorithm engine
description: Evolve decoded bridge genomes using deterministic randomness, fitness from the agreed mechanics contract, elitism, parent selection, crossover, and mutation. Keep generation transitions independent of UI state.
design: Use an explicit seeded PRNG rather than Math.random. Start with tournament selection, one or two elites, and per-gene mutation; choose conservative defaults (e.g. population 24) but keep them configurable. Keep the GA pure and deterministic.
acceptance_criteria: A seed reproduces the same initial population and subsequent generations; selection ranks by maximum stable load with the agreed tie-break; elites survive unchanged; crossover and mutation produce valid budget-bounded genomes; population size remains fixed; unit tests demonstrate fitness does not depend on render timing.
close_reason: Implemented seed-based initial populations, tournament selection, uniform crossover, bit mutation, elitism, budget/connectivity normalization, and stable fitness ordering; GA tests pass.

title: Define bridge lattice, genome encoding, and viable seeds
description: Represent legal one-stick members and candidate bridge structures on the fixed-span lattice. Define deterministic genome decode/encode and a first-generation strategy that includes valid load-bearing structures as well as diverse variants.
design: Keep the genome representation independent from Canvas and the solver. Favor a compact bitset/edge-vector over all legal unit-stick edges, with bounded heights and explicit support/deck constraints. Include known truss patterns in the seed population so early generations can demonstrate meaningful results rather than all scoring zero.
acceptance_criteria: Genome decoding is deterministic for a seed; members map to legal lattice edges and never exceed the shared stick budget; endpoint supports and center load node are represented explicitly; invalid/disconnected/mechanism structures are detectable; initial candidates include viable bridges and varied topologies.
close_reason: Implemented one-stick triangular-lattice topology, mandatory deck/support/load nodes, deterministic binary genomes, valid baseline trusses, diverse deterministic seeds, budget handling, and connectivity validation.

title: Implement deterministic truss solve and progressive failure
description: Implement a pure, deterministic structural evaluator for a candidate bridge under an increasing center load. Solve nodal equilibrium/member axial force, identify tension or compression-buckling failure, remove failed sticks, and redistribute load until the bridge is stable or collapses.
design: Use a small 2D linear-elastic truss stiffness solver. Make the load ramp event-driven: calculate the next load at which a capacity is reached, break/re-solve, and expose those events for smooth visual animation. This preserves the steady rising-weight experience without recomputing a dense solve for every animation frame. Treat glue joints as idealized pins in v1.
acceptance_criteria: Known small trusses produce expected reactions and member-force signs; unstable/singular structures fail safely; both tension and compression limits are enforced; broken members are removed and load is re-solved/cascaded; repeated evaluation of the same bridge and parameters returns the same failure load and break sequence.
close_reason: Implemented the pure 2D truss stiffness solve, support reactions, event-driven tension/buckling thresholds, member removal and redistribution, and deterministic collapse results; manually verified a known triangle and failure cases.

title: Agree on v1 bridge mechanics and fitness contract
description:
## Decision
Proposed v1 contract: build a deterministic client-side 2D pin-jointed truss simulation on a one-toothpick lattice. Use a pinned left support, roller right support, a centered hanging load, a shared finite stick budget, idealized glue joints, and axial tension/compression-buckling limits. Remove failed members and re-solve so load can cascade. Score maximum stable load in kg-equivalent at Earth gravity, with stick count as a tie-break. This decision remains open until the project owner confirms the assumptions.

## Rationale
This preserves the satisfying rising-weight/failure animation while making bridge topology and failure scores deterministic, fast to compare across a genetic population, and easy to test. The model is explicitly educational, not a structural safety calculator.

## Alternatives Considered
- Rigid-body physics only: visually dynamic, but it does not provide a credible deterministic strength score for toothpick trusses.
- Full engineering/finite-element analysis: too broad and costly for the first web prototype, and would invite misleading real-world precision.
- Purely decorative load animation: simplest, but it would make genetic fitness arbitrary rather than tied to bridge mechanics.
design: Recommended defaults: each edge is one equal-length toothpick; all joints are ideal pins with no glue failure; supports are left pin/right roller; the weight hangs from the center deck node; linear static truss analysis uses Earth gravity and displays kg-equivalent load; members fail in tension or compression/buckling; after a member breaks, solve again and cascade until stable or globally unstable. The score is the maximum stable load with a shared per-bridge stick budget. This is a toy model and must not be presented as a real build/safety calculator.
acceptance_criteria: The bridge geometry, supports, load position/units, stick budget, member and joint failure assumptions, failure/cascade rule, fitness/tie-break rule, and educational disclaimer are written down and accepted. Implementation beads can then proceed without changing the evaluation contract midstream.
close_reason: Owner approved the proposed deterministic static truss approach, idealized joints, shared stick budget, progressive failure, and educational framing.

title: Build an interactive genetic toothpick bridge lab
description: Create a client-side web experience inspired by the interaction loop of red42/HTML5_Genetic_Cars: visualize candidate designs, test them, evolve a population, and inspect best results. The primary simulation is a toothpick truss bridge with a hanging center load that increases until structural failure. Keep the mechanics deterministic and educational rather than claiming engineering-grade accuracy.
design: Static client-only app using native JavaScript modules, HTML/CSS, and Canvas 2D. Fixed 8-toothpick support span, 10 deck bays, 11 deck nodes, and 10 evolvable upper joints; a 20-value Uint16 genome sets each apex offset and height. Keep a connected triangulated 2D pin-jointed truss with 39 segments and a hard 40-toothpick budget; each segment consumes one whole toothpick regardless of length, and all member/triangle sides remain below one toothpick. Left pin, right roller, centered load. The deterministic solver uses actual member lengths for axial stiffness and compression buckling. Finite glue failures use an explicit configurable lap-joint approximation (default 0.44x of 120 N wood tension; source range is cross-product, not a product-specific Elmer's rating), and event records identify wood versus glue failure. Seeded GA, score by maximum stable load (kg-equivalent), animate/replay, population/history, speed/pause/step, seed, and local versioned save/restore. Document the educational limits; do not present scores as engineering predictions.
acceptance_criteria: A visitor can watch a seeded population of bridges undergo load-to-failure tests, see how each generation improves, inspect/replay the strongest bridge, and control or restart an evolution run. The model limitations are visible in the product documentation.
close_reason: Completed the client-side Bridge Lab, including geometry evolution, sub-toothpick member validation, 40-stick budget, finite illustrative glue-joint model, persistence, responsive UI, and automated/browser verification.

title: Add a Surprise mode for rapid multi-generation evolution
description: The current Fast-forward generation button marks only the current generation complete. Add a distinct Surprise-style mode inspired by Genetic Cars: suppress or greatly reduce drawing so the simulation can run much faster across successive generations, rather than stopping after one generation.
design: The reference's Surprise control is described as toggling drawing to make the simulation faster. In Bridge Lab, distinguish this from both Fast-forward generation (complete one generation's visual tests) and the 1–8× playback speed setting (faster load animation). Provide a clear reversible mode that runs/continues evolution across generations with canvas rendering throttled or skipped, while keeping generation, best/average, and tested-count feedback understandable. Allow pause/exit back to normal visualization at any time. Rendering choices must not affect scores or seeded GA results.
acceptance_criteria: A clearly labeled and keyboard-accessible Surprise control starts or toggles rapid evolution that progresses through multiple generations without requiring per-generation clicks. It visibly indicates its active state, can be stopped/paused promptly, and restores normal visualization afterward. It is distinct from current-generation fast-forward and the playback speed slider. With the same seed/settings, fast and normally rendered runs produce identical generation scores/genomes; tests cover mode transitions, pause/resume, progress/history, and determinism.
notes: Reference inspected: https://rednuht.org/genetic_cars_2/ describes Surprise as toggling drawing to make the simulation faster. Current handleFastForward() only completes the current generation; normal continuous evolution animates every candidate and uses a 900 ms inter-generation delay. The separate 8× playback request is tracked in tbv-rs1 and should remain available.

title: Allow test playback up to 8× speed
description: The user would like to accelerate load-test animation to 8×. The current speed range is 1–5× and the playback helper and saved-run validation also clamp/reject values above 5×.
design: Extend the existing speed slider and playback mapping to 8×. At the current 3600 ms base duration this corresponds to about 450 ms per test, while reduced-motion behavior remains unchanged. Speed must only affect visualization duration, never the evaluated bridge score or genetic reproducibility. Preserve valid saved settings and accept 8× on save/restore.
acceptance_criteria: The UI offers 1× through 8× and reports the selected speed. An 8× test/replay completes in the expected shorter duration; speed 1–8 is accepted by playback and persistence, and reduced-motion duration remains accessible. Tests verify speed does not alter evaluation results and saved runs round-trip an 8× setting.
notes: Code paths to update include index.html #speed-control, src/playback.mjs loadTestDurationMs clamp, src/persistence.mjs saved speed validation, app readout/restore, and playback/persistence tests.

title: Display bridge loads to hundredths of a kilogram
description: Result labels currently round kg-equivalent loads to one decimal, making close candidates (for example, values around 1.4 kg) look tied. The genetic algorithm already ranks using unrounded maxStableLoadN, so this is primarily a presentation and inspection-resolution issue, not a fitness-precision defect.
design: Show two decimal places anywhere users compare completed results: candidate cards, leaderboard, best/average summary, history labels, and tested-bridge status/caption. Keep transient animated load labels concise if needed. Never round stored loads or fitness comparisons; retain deterministic full-precision force values internally.
acceptance_criteria: Two candidates whose unrounded kg-equivalent scores differ but both display as 1.4 at one decimal are visibly distinguishable to hundredths in the comparison surfaces. Ranking order continues to use raw maxStableLoadN and is covered by a regression test. Update relevant accessible labels/history text and keep desktop/mobile layouts usable.
notes: Verified in src/genetics.mjs: loadFitness reads result.maxStableLoadN directly and compareEvaluations sorts on that raw value; rounding occurs in src/ui.mjs and src/app.mjs via toFixed(1). Therefore the GA already distinguishes values below a tenth; expose that precision visually without quantizing fitness.

title: Add population-diversity telemetry and exploration controls
description: The 24-member GA population becomes visually/genetically homogeneous after only a few generations. Current defaults include two elites, tournament size 3, an exposed mutation probability (1–30%, default 8%), and a fixed mutation step range. Measure convergence and add user-facing ways to encourage exploration without compromising seeded reproducibility.
design: First expose what the mutation code currently hides: mutation magnitude, alongside the existing mutation probability. Consider a simple selection-pressure control (tournament size) and a visible diversity signal (unique genome count or normalized gene distance). Start with telemetry and understandable controls; avoid full speciation for the 24-member population unless seeded experiments show these simpler controls/occasional immigrants are insufficient. Persist/restore any new settings and keep generation outcomes deterministic for a fixed seed and settings.
acceptance_criteria: The UI reports a meaningful current-generation diversity metric. Users can adjust mutation magnitude and selection pressure in addition to mutation probability; labels/hints explain their effects. Settings round-trip through local save/restore, and identical seeds/settings reproduce genomes and scores. Add deterministic tests over multi-generation seeded runs showing how controls affect diversity/convergence, and document whether the evidence warrants a separate speciation mechanism.
notes: Potential user-level controls: mutation chance (already exposed), mutation strength (currently a fixed 3,000–12,000 gene delta), tournament size/selection pressure (currently fixed at 3), and possibly population size or a small random-immigrant fraction if a compact UI permits. Recommendation to validate with diversity telemetry before implementing species clustering/fitness sharing, which adds complexity and can split a small population.

title: Explore a two-tier truss within the 40-toothpick budget
description: Revisit the earlier two-row triangular lattice as a possible bridge option. The current evolved topology uses 39 fixed members (10 deck segments, 20 legs, 9 upper chords) and guarantees every segment is strictly shorter than one toothpick. Determine whether a useful second triangle tier can be restored while preserving the fixed 8-toothpick span, strict per-segment length bound, and 40-segment maximum; if so, implement a valid selectable/evolvable topology.
design: Do a member/node count before coding. The deck needs at least nine segments across the 8-unit span under the strict <1 rule. Compare a full second tier against a partial/optional central roof module and other redesigned layouts. The old rows=2 implementation in dcfe871 used one-unit deck members, so it is a reference only, not proof that the new constraints fit. Do not silently relax the toothpick budget or length invariant.
acceptance_criteria: Provide a checked node/member count for the proposed topology. If feasible, include at least one deterministic two-tier candidate whose every member and triangle side is <1, whose member count is <=40, and whose load path is connected and statically solvable; add geometry, budget, and solver regression tests. If a full-span second tier cannot fit, document a counted lower bound and the smallest useful partial-tier compromise that does fit, with tests for its constraints.
notes: The previous fixed-lattice version supported rows=2 with optional edges, but some deck sticks had length exactly one. The current variable geometry replaced it with a 39-member minimally triangulated topology. Preserve all current constraints while exploring the user's request for the former two levels of triangles.

title: Verify accessibility, responsive behavior, and runtime performance
description: Run integrated smoke checks and refine the experience across desktop and small-screen sizes, keyboard navigation, and reduced motion. Ensure evaluating a generation does not freeze the page.
design: If generation evaluation exceeds a responsive frame budget, move pure GA/solver evaluation to a Web Worker while keeping deterministic input/output and the same test coverage.
acceptance_criteria: Core controls are labeled and keyboard reachable; canvas information has an accessible textual equivalent; contrast and focus states are usable; reduced-motion behavior is respected; a full generation completes without a long main-thread stall; smoke-test steps are recorded.
notes:
Automated QA completed: npm test passes (22 tests, including worker protocol and accessibility markup); JavaScript syntax and HTML ID/selector checks pass; local HTTP smoke checks returned 200 for the page and every module. A 24-bridge direct evaluation measured about 49 ms, so generation evaluation now runs in a module worker. Manual visual/keyboard/responsive browser smoke remains outstanding; browser automation was avoided per user preference, and the steps are documented in README.
Headless Chromium end-to-end smoke completed without pire-browser: module-worker initialization rendered all 24 cards; Tab reached Step with visible focus and Space activated it; the population advanced to 1/24; fast-forward completed generation 1 and populated the 5-entry leaderboard/history; save, new run, and restore worked. At 375×812 there was no horizontal overflow (document and body 375 px; controls ended at 348 px); desktop render checked at 1440 px. Emulated reduced motion completed the first bridge in 189 ms. No browser console/runtime errors after adding a local SVG favicon. Screenshot inspection led to moving the span annotation away from the mobile legend.
close_reason: Automated tests and Chromium desktop/mobile, keyboard, reduced-motion, evolution, and persistence smoke checks passed.

title: Document usage, model limits, and project commands
description: Explain how to run the static site, how the genetic loop and bridge scoring work, and where the approximation differs from real toothpick construction.
design: Inspect source inspiration at https://github.com/red42/HTML5_Genetic_Cars; borrow interaction concepts (seeded runs, controls, replay, score history), not code/assets unless licensing and attribution are deliberately handled.
acceptance_criteria: README explains local serving, controls, seed/reproducibility, tests, fitness, supports/load/member assumptions, and explicitly warns that the app is educational and not a structural safety calculator; any borrowed ideas/assets are attributed and license-compatible.
close_reason: README now documents running, controls, reproducible GA, model/scoring assumptions, limitations, attribution, and manual smoke steps.

title: Show population gallery, rankings, and generation trends
description: Present candidate bridges and their test outcomes in a compact population view, alongside best/average performance over generations and a selectable leaderboard.
design: Keep a clear route between the animated single-bridge stage and the whole population: candidates can be tested sequentially in the stage while completed candidates accumulate results in the gallery. Offer a fast-forward mode for evaluation runs.
acceptance_criteria: Each current-generation candidate has an identifiable thumbnail/status and failure-load result; selecting a candidate displays it in the main stage; best and average load history are plotted with labeled axes; the current champion and generation are obvious; empty and first-generation states are handled.
close_reason: Added selectable bridge thumbnails, per-candidate test status/load, top-five leaderboard, current champion highlighting, best/average generation history, and accessible chart descriptions.

title: Wire evolution controls and reproducible run settings
description: Connect the app to the simulation and GA with controls for starting/pausing, stepping, changing playback speed, fast-forwarding, choosing a seed, and starting a fresh population. Expose only useful v1 parameters without overwhelming the experience.
design: Keep a small default surface: run/pause, next/step, speed, new run/seed, mutation rate, and optional save/restore. Avoid adding unsupported physics knobs before the underlying model is validated.
acceptance_criteria: Pause/resume preserves the current load event; step advances one candidate or generation predictably; fast-forward completes evaluation without changing scores; reset with the same seed recreates the same run; settings changes have clear apply/reset behavior; controls work by keyboard.
close_reason: Wired pause/resume, one-bridge stepping, fast-forward, replay, seeded reset, speed/mutation sliders, keyboard-native controls, and generation advancement; pause preserves in-flight load progress.

title: Scaffold the static workshop UI and responsive layout
description: Build the no-build-step app shell for the bridge lab. Establish the visual language and responsive page regions before wiring the simulation.
design: Use warm toothpick/joint colors against a high-contrast workshop backdrop. Keep all controls as semantic HTML; reserve Canvas 2D for bridge rendering and graphs. Structure code into small native ES modules so the model remains testable independently of the DOM.
acceptance_criteria: The app opens from a local static server with no runtime framework/dependency; the layout includes a canvas stage, controls/metrics region, population area, and generation-history area; the interface remains usable on narrow screens and respects reduced-motion preferences.
close_reason: Implemented the dependency-free responsive workshop shell, semantic controls, accessible Canvas regions, reduced-motion CSS, and local static serving.

title: Save and restore evolution runs locally
description: Persist a run snapshot in browser localStorage so users can return to a seed, population, settings, and champion without a backend.
design: Persist plain serializable state only (seed, GA settings, genomes, generation history, selected champion); do not serialize Canvas or live solver objects. Provide a clear reset/delete action.
acceptance_criteria: Users can save and restore a run; stored data is versioned and validated; invalid or obsolete data produces a recoverable message; no bridge/run data is sent to a server.
close_reason: Added versioned localStorage snapshots with topology/model validation, genome revalidation, progress/settings/history restore, clear/delete action, and recoverable errors; persistence tests pass.
